result.summary: Thetis displays Achilles' arms, and Aias and Odysseus contend for them before Trojan captives, who award them to Odysseus. Athena drives Aias mad; he slaughters sheep, recovers his senses and kills himself. The Greeks mourn, burn him on a pyre and raise a mound.

scenes.title: The Shield and Arms Displayed
scenes.summary: Thetis lays out Achilles' arms, and the scenes on the shield are described in detail.

place.name: the Argive camp by the ships

scenes.title: Thetis Offers the Arms
scenes.summary: Thetis offers the arms to the one who saved Achilles' body. Aias and Odysseus claim them, and Nestor persuades the kings to let Trojan captives judge.
scenes.stakes: The kings risk the lasting anger of whichever hero loses.

place.name: the Argive camp by the ships

scenes.title: The Contest of Words
scenes.summary: Aias and Odysseus trade boasts and insults. The Trojans award the arms to Odysseus.
scenes.stakes: Honour and Achilles' arms, the prize for the greatest hero.

place.name: the Argive camp by the ships

scenes.title: Aias Stunned; Nereids Mourn
scenes.summary: Aias freezes in grief and is led to the ships. Thetis and the Nereids rage at Prometheus while the Argives sleep.

scenes.title: Madness of Aias
scenes.summary: Athena strikes Aias with madness to save Odysseus. He rages through the camp and slaughters sheep as Sleep and Hera pass overhead.
scenes.stakes: Aias is destroying himself; the Greeks fear for their ships and lives.

place.name: the Argive camp by the ships

scenes.title: Awakening and Despair
scenes.summary: Teucer and Agamemnon fear Aias. Athena lifts the madness, and Aias sees what he has done and laments.
scenes.stakes: Aias's honour and will to live.

place.name: the Argive camp by the ships

scenes.title: Death and Lament of Aias
scenes.summary: Aias kills himself with Hector's sword. Teucer and Tecmessa mourn, Agamemnon promises protection, and Odysseus laments.
scenes.stakes: Tecmessa and her son face slavery; the Greeks lose their defender.

place.name: the Argive camp by the ships

scenes.title: Funeral Pyre and Mound
scenes.summary: Nestor urges them to funeral rites. Aias is burned, his bones are buried in a mound at Rhoeteium, and the Greeks sleep uneasily.
scenes.stakes: The Greeks fear a Trojan attack now that Aias is dead.

alias_notes.explanation: Son of Cronus, a title of Zeus.
Pallas is an epithet of Athena; the text uses both names.

notable_quotes.reason: Odysseus's creed that wit accomplishes all things.
Aias's bitter complaint before his suicide that the brave go unrewarded.
Odysseus's moral: the wise endure ills without raging at fate.

analysis.text: The book sets brute strength against cunning and shows how wounded honour and wrath destroy even the greatest warrior.
The story of the judgement of the arms and Aias's suicide was told in lost early epics and by Sophocles; this retelling follows the epic tradition, with Trojan captives as judges.

legacy.text: Sophocles' tragedy Ajax dramatises the madness and suicide of Aias, and the episode shaped later literature, including Ovid's Metamorphoses, where Ajax and Ulysses argue for the arms.

fun_facts.text: This poem is by Quintus of Smyrna, a Greek epic poet of perhaps the 3rd or 4th century AD, who continued the story after Homer's Iliad.

language_notes.text: The Fire-god is Hephaestus, divine smith. Aeacus' son is Peleus, Achilles' father; the shield is described as made for Achilles, Peleus' son, who is meant here by the phrase's context.
"Thou hadst said" means "you would have said": the work was so lifelike that birds seemed alive.
Tethys is a sea goddess, wife of Ocean, whose stream was imagined as encircling the world.
Enyo is a goddess of war; the Avenging Spirits are the Furies-like Keres, spirits of violent death.
"Glebe" means soil or plowed field; "wains" are wagons.
Cypris is Aphrodite, called so from Cyprus; she was born from sea foam.
The Nereids lead their sister Thetis to her wedding with Peleus on Mount Pelion.
"Earth-shaker" is the epithet of Poseidon, god of sea and earthquakes.
"Peleides" means son of Peleus, i.e. Achilles.
"Sable-stoled" means dressed in black robes, the colour of mourning; "stole" here is a long robe.
"The blessed Deathless" means the immortal gods.
"Laertes' seed" is Odysseus, son of Laertes; "Telamon's son" is Aias. Both are named by their fathers.
"Weened" is archaic for thought or supposed.
"Passing-wise" means surpassingly wise.
"Corse" is an archaic word for corpse.
"Thralls" are slaves or captives; "spear-won" means taken in war.
"Dam" means mother, usually used of animals, which makes the insult harsher. "Craven" means coward.
Aias refers to the story that Odysseus tried to avoid the war by feigning madness until the sons of Atreus (Agamemnon and Menelaus) forced him to go.
Poeas' son is Philoctetes, abandoned on Lemnos because of his festering snake-bite wound; Aias blames Odysseus's counsel.
Palamedes was a Greek hero who, in legend, was destroyed by Odysseus's trickery, framed as a traitor.
"Chode" is an old past tense of "chide": he scolded or rebuked.
"Niddering" is an archaic word for a base, cowardly person.
Oeneus' valiant son is Diomedes, who went with Odysseus on a night raid toward Hector's watchmen.
"Rede" means counsel or advice; "suasive" means persuasive.
Odysseus recalls the wrestling match at Patroclus' funeral games, where he and Aias fought to a draw.
"Wilderment" means bewilderment, a confused, dazed state of mind.
The "filmy veil 'twixt bone and brain" is the membrane around the brain; 'twixt means "betwixt," between.
"Doom" is personified as a pursuer; the line says this is Aias' last walk along that path before his death.
Prometheus foretold that Thetis's son would be greater than his father. Zeus therefore married her to the mortal Peleus instead of taking her himself.
Prometheus was punished by Zeus: chained to a rock while an eagle ate his liver, which grew back daily. Cymothoe wishes the torment on him.
"Tare" is an archaic past tense of "tear"; "aye" means ever or always.
"Pallas" is a name for Athena, here called by the title Pallas.
The Pleiades setting before Orion marks the stormy season; the stars "flee" the hunter Orion and plunge into Ocean.
Sleep (Hypnos) helped Hera deceive Zeus on Mount Ida in the Iliad, so Hera is grateful to him.
"Cronion" means son of Cronos, a title of Zeus. "Marriage-kin" refers to Sleep's marriage tie with Hera.
"Would God" is an archaic wish formula, meaning "I wish to God that..."; Thetis is the one who set the arms as a prize.
Laertes' son is Odysseus (here called Ulysses elsewhere in some translations), who competed with Aias for Achilles' arms and won them.
Aeacus' son is Achilles, grandson of Aeacus; his death left Aias as the Greeks' chief defender.
The resourceful king of the Cephallenian folk is Odysseus, ruler of Cephallenia and neighboring islands.
"Blood-boltered" means with hair matted with blood.
The Erinnyes are the Furies, avenging spirits who punish wrongdoers and arrogant men.
"Consort" here means to keep company or associate with.
"Guerdon" means reward or recompense.
Typhon was a monstrous giant who challenged the gods; Zeus struck him down with thunderbolts. Note the translation here uses Zeus, elsewhere Jove-style names are avoided.
Danaans: a name for the Greeks, from the legendary king Danaus. Achaeans and Argives are used the same way.
"Bale" means evil, ruin or woe; "murder and bale" means deadly harm.
Tecmessa was a captive taken in war, yet Aias made her his wife; the bride-price lines say she held a wife's full authority.
"The Unseen Land" is a euphemism for the underworld, the realm of the dead.
The arms of Achilles were awarded to Odysseus rather than Aias after a contest, which drove Aias to rage and madness.
"Meed" means a due reward or prize; here, the honour of winning the arms.
Neleus' son is Nestor, the aged king of Pylos; the epithet by patronymic replaces his name.
"All unmeet" means wholly improper or unfitting; "dues beseeming" are the rites suited to the dead.
"Kine" is an old plural for cattle; "vests" here means garments or robes.
Phaethon, son of the Sun, died driving his father's chariot. His sisters, the Heliades, wept beside the river Eridanus and were turned into poplars, their tears into amber.

Enceladus was a Giant buried under Sicily (Thrinacia) after defeating by Zeus' thunderbolt ("levin"). Hercules burned himself on Mount Oeta after Nessus' poisoned shirt tormented him, and became a god.
Rhoeteium is a headland on the Trojan coast near the Greek camp, where Aias' tomb stood.
"Child of the Mist" is a poetic name for Dawn, which follows the dark and mist of night.

context_notes.text: Thetis, Achilles' divine mother, offers the arms as prize for the Greek judged best after his death; Aias and Ulysses compete.
The helmet shows the war of Zeus and the Olympians against the Titans, for rule of the universe.
Achilles killed the Trojan prince Hector with this spear, from the Greek ash-wood of Mount Pelion.
Thetis is a sea goddess, Achilles' mother. She had set funeral games for her dead son, in which prizes were won.
Aias (Ajax) was the greatest Greek warrior after Achilles. He carried Achilles' body from the battle.
Hesperus is the evening star. Peleides means son of Peleus, i.e. Achilles, whose arms Aias now claims.
Nestor is the oldest Greek king, known for wise counsel. Atreus' son is Agamemnon, the Greek commander.
Thetis, a sea goddess, was Achilles' mother. She set Achilles' arms as the prize for the bravest Greek.
A folkmote is a public assembly. Aias says words belong there, not in deciding who is the better warrior.
Peleides means son of Peleus, that is, Achilles' son Neoptolemus is not meant here; the name refers to Achilles' line, and Odysseus claims to have brought him to the war.
Odysseus claims descent from Zeus, as Achilles' ancestry also traces to him.
Thetis is a sea goddess, one of the Nereids, daughters of Nereus, and the mother of Achilles.
Idomeneus was king of Crete and a Greek leader at Troy.
Athena favours Odysseus, who is her protégé, and in the tradition she drives Aias mad after he lost the contest for Achilles' armour.
Pasithea is one of the Graces, the goddess promised to Sleep as his bride in the Iliad.
Aias attacks the sheep believing they are the Greek leaders; the flock is the Argives' captured livestock.
Thetis, Achilles' sea-goddess mother, set his armor as a prize for the bravest Greek, which led to the dispute between Aias and Odysseus.
Danaans is another name for the Greeks.
The Xanthus is the river of the Trojan plain, near which the Greek camp lay.
Teucer is Aias's half-brother, an archer, and also a son of Telamon.
Salamis is the island kingdom of Telamon, Aias's father, and the home of Teucer.
Eurysaces, whose name means "broad shield," is the infant son of Aias and Tecmessa.
Agamemnon is the commander of the Greek army; his promise gives Tecmessa protection from slavery.
Washing and wrapping the body in linen was the normal preparation of the dead before cremation.
Thetis is the sea-goddess and mother of Achilles; she sends the wind to help the pyre burn.
Quenching the pyre with wine and gathering the bones into a golden container follows Homeric funeral custom.

literary_notes.text: The craftsmanship is praised as so real that metal birds seem to live and float on the breeze.
Panic, Dread, Strife and Enyo appear as figures, making the abstract horrors of war vivid.
War's horrors are set against the works of peace, dividing the shield into two contrasting worlds.
The narrator's aside "It all seemed real" insists on the illusion of life in the divine art.
Ocean clasping the rim like a garland frames the whole shield as a world encircled by water.
The spear still reeking of Hector's blood recalls Achilles' past victory in a grim final image.
Aias is compared to Hesperus outshining the stars, showing his splendour and superiority among the Greeks in Achilles' armour.
"This in war, and that in counsel" contrasts Aias' strength with Odysseus' wisdom, summarising their rivalry.
Nestor praises his own age and experience, as the aged counsellor typically does, establishing his authority.
The Greeks will let their enslaved enemies judge, trusting that hatred of both Greeks gives fairness.
Odysseus as a cur and Aias as a thunder-voiced lion makes the contrast between them vivid and insulting.
The repeated "Thou--thou" hammers home Aias's contempt and his claim that Odysseus feared Hector.
The list of rocks, seas, beasts and bulls conquered by skill builds Odysseus's argument that wit beats brute strength.
Trojans fleeing Aias are compared to geese or cranes scattering from an eagle, making his boast of dominance vivid.
Odysseus's joy meets the Greeks' groan, hinting at the tragic consequences of the award, especially for Aias.
Comparing Aias to a statue conveys his rigid, numb shock.
Doom is portrayed as a figure following close behind Aias, foreshadowing his suicide.
An extended storm comparison, with stars and sea, shows the scale of Aias' destructive fury.
Aias is likened to a bereaved lioness-like beast, then to a boiling cauldron, to convey rage born of loss.
Repeated "Like" piles up images of sea, storm and fire, intensifying the madness.
The mighty hero slaughters helpless sheep while believing he is killing his enemies, the Danaans.
The cowering shepherds are compared to hares hiding from an eagle, conveying Aias's predatory terror.
Aias mocks a slaughtered ram as if it were Odysseus; the reader knows his delusion while he does not.
Madness is a fiend that Athena tears away and which flees to the Styx, treating it as a creature.
Aias is likened to a rooted mountain rock, showing his paralysed, immovable horror.
Aias's bitter complaint about forgotten deeds shows his wounded pride and sense of injustice.
Aias fallen in the dust is compared to the giant Typhon blasted by thunderbolts, giving his death mythic scale.
The earth groans and has a breast, as if she mourns and receives the fallen hero.
The cries of the Greeks are likened to ewes bleating around pens after their lambs are taken, expressing helpless loss.
Teucer's weeping is compared to an orphan child's wailing beside the hearth, stressing his desolation.
Tecmessa's address to the dead Aias and her wish for the earth to open express raw grief.
Suffering is compared to a flood coming from every side, conveying the orphan's helplessness.
Odysseus shows humane reflection, blaming wrath rather than gloating over his rival's death.
Fate's sorrows are "stroke after stroke", as blows rained on the Greeks, making grief a repeated assault.
The Fates are "ruthless" and "swallow" the dead in night, presenting death as a devouring creature.
Aias' burning is compared to Enceladus and Hercules, lending the pyre mythic scale and hinting at heroic apotheosis.
The brief, balanced line sets Trojan joy against Achaean grief, showing how one death divides the two armies.
The Greeks' dread of a night attack, now Aias is dead, hints at their weakened position and coming troubles.
